opus-5.5.text:
What excites me most is that we're learning these worlds without any action labels. Traditionally, if you wanted to train a world model, you needed data where you knew what action was taken at every step: the agent pressed "jump," and here's what the next frame looked like. That kind of data is expensive and pretty limited. But the internet is full of videos of people playing games, robots moving around, all sorts of dynamic scenes, and none of that comes with action annotations.

With Genie, the idea was to learn a latent action space directly from the videos themselves. The model has to figure out, in an unsupervised way, which changes between frames are consistent and controllable, things like moving left, moving right, or jumping. Once you have that, you can take an image the model has never seen before, even a sketch someone drew or a photo, and turn it into something you can actually step through and interact with.

For me that's really exciting because it opens up a path to scaling. If we can learn controllable environments from the huge amount of unlabeled video out there, we're no longer bottlenecked by hand-designed simulators or carefully collected action datasets. And longer term, I think that matters a lot for training generalist agents. You could imagine generating an almost endless variety of environments for agents to learn in, and potentially using these latent actions to help agents learn behaviors by watching videos, much like people learn a lot by watching others.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. I think the thing that excites me most is that we didn't tell it anything about actions. That's really the core of it. We trained Genie on a lot of internet gameplay videos, and there are no labels in that data about what the player was doing, there's no controller input, nothing. It's just frames. And out of that, the model learned a latent action space on its own, where you can press, say, "action three" and the character moves right, or jumps, and that same action does something consistent across totally different scenes and even in images the model has never seen.

What makes that exciting to me is that action labels are usually the bottleneck. If you want to train an agent or a world model, you typically need data where someone recorded what was done at each step, and that's expensive and it doesn't scale. But there's an enormous amount of video in the world where people are doing things, and historically that data has been kind of unusable for learning controllable models. Genie is a step toward unlocking that.

And then the interactive part is the other half. It's not just predicting what the next frame looks like, it's letting you step in and drive. You can draw a sketch, or hand it a photograph, and suddenly you have a little playable environment. For me, coming from a reinforcement learning background, that's the dream, because it means you could in principle generate endless training environments for agents without anyone hand-designing them. We're still at an early stage, the worlds are low resolution and the action space is small, but the fact that this emerges at all from unlabeled video is what really gets me going.

astra-6.text:
What excites me most is the possibility of learning how a world works just by watching it, and then being able to interact with what you've learned. Video gives you observations, but it doesn't necessarily tell you what action caused a particular change. So learning a representation that lets you control what happens next is a really interesting step.

From a reinforcement learning perspective, that opens up the possibility of learning environments from video that an agent could then practice in. You could imagine showing it examples of different settings and giving it opportunities to explore, rather than having to hand-design every environment. The big question is how well those learned worlds capture the consequences of actions, but that potential to turn passive observations into interactive experience is what I find exciting.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me most is the possibility of turning passive video into something an agent can actually interact with. A video shows you what happened, but an interactive world model lets you ask, “What would happen if I took a different action?” That opens up a really interesting way to learn through experimentation.

And the fact that Genie can learn this without being given the actions associated with each video is particularly exciting. It suggests a path toward building environments from much more widely available data, where we could eventually train and evaluate agents across a much broader range of experiences. The big question is how well those learned interactions capture the things an agent needs to understand about the world.
